Diffusion and Diffusion Policy

A map from demonstrations to sampled action chunks

Known Gaussian corruption supplies a noise target; regression learns a predictor for reverse sampling.

$$\E\|Y-g(X)\|^2$$
$X$
noisy demonstrated action sequence together with its diffusion level
$Y$
Gaussian noise deliberately drawn to corrupt that sequence

trainable rule that predicts noise from the noisy input

DDPM §§2–3; Diffusion Policy §2.3; course concept map · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Motivation

Multimodal actions

Two valid actions can have an invalid mean

A multimodal distribution has several distinct regions of high probability.

$$P(A=-2\mid o)=P(A=2\mid o)=\tfrac12$$
$A$
scalar route choice; −2 left, +2 right
$o$
fixed obstacle observation

Diffusion Policy §4.1 · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Derivation

Multimodal actions

Squared error selects a conditional mean

Squared-error risk is the expected squared prediction error; assume a finite second moment.

$$\E[(A-u)^2\mid o]=\operatorname{Var}(A\mid o)+(u-\E[A\mid o])^2$$
$u$
chosen scalar prediction
$A,o$
random action; fixed observation
$\operatorname{Var}(A\mid o)$
action spread at this observation

The squared-error minimizer is $u^*=\mathbb E[A\mid o]$; a mean can lie between valid modes.

Derivation 1 / 2

Expand around the conditional mean

Fix $o$. Let $m=\E[A\mid o]$; $u$ is a scalar prediction. Assume a finite second moment.

  1. $A-u=(A-m)+(m-u)$.
  2. $(A-u)^2=(A-m)^2+2(A-m)(m-u)+(m-u)^2$.
  3. $\E[A-m\mid o]=0$, so the averaged cross term is zero.

Derivation 2 / 2

Only one term depends on the prediction

$m$ is fixed when $u$ changes.

  1. $\E[(A-u)^2\mid o]=\operatorname{Var}(A\mid o)+(m-u)^2$.
  2. The variance is independent of u; the remaining square is minimized at zero.
  3. Thus $u^*=m=\E[A\mid o]$.

DL §3.8; course derivation · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Example

Multimodal actions

Worked example: the average misses both modes

Example

$$R(u)=\tfrac12(u+2)^2+\tfrac12(u-2)^2=u^2+4$$
$R(u)$
expected squared error for A=−2 or +2, each with probability 1/2
$u$
chosen scalar action

Diffusion Policy §4.1; course example · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Exercise

Multimodal actions

Transfer: one route is more common

Find the squared-error minimizer u; compare it with the mode (most probable action).

$$P(A=-2\mid o)=\tfrac34,\quad P(A=2\mid o)=\tfrac14$$
$A$
random action at fixed observation o
$u$
deterministic prediction to optimize

Check $u^*=-1$; a mean need not be a mode.

Solution 1 / 1

Choose the conditional mean

$A$ is the random action; $u$ is a deterministic prediction.

  1. Squared error is minimized by $u^*=\E[A\mid o]$.
  2. $u^*=\tfrac34(-2)+\tfrac14(2)=-\tfrac32+\tfrac12=-1$.
  3. The mode is -2, while the minimum-risk mean is -1.

DL §3.8; course exercise · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Exercise

Multimodal actions

A distribution and its mean answer different questions

Fixed observation; equally likely actions -2 and 2.
Compare: conditional mean vs a random draw.

Check Sampling preserves the two choices.

Solution 1 / 1

Compare the operations

$A$ is drawn from the two-point action distribution.

  1. $\E[A\mid o]=0$: averaging returns one fixed value.
  2. $A\sim p(\cdot\mid o)$: sampling returns -2 or 2, each with probability one half.
  3. A correct distribution can still have an unusable mean.

Motivation

Forward diffusion

Noise creates a supervised learning task

Denoising estimates clean-data information from an artificially corrupted input.

DDPM §2, Algorithms 1–2 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Model

Forward diffusion

Two clocks and three kinds of vectors

The diffusion index labels corruption levels of one stored vector; physical time labels robot execution.

$$x_0,x_k,\epsilon\in\mathbb R^d,\quad k\in\{1,\ldots,K\}$$
$x_0,x_k∈R^d$
clean/noisy column vectors with d components
$k,K$
diffusion index and final level
$r,ε$
physical time; standard Gaussian noise

DDPM §2; Diffusion Policy §2.3 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Definition

Forward diffusion

One step shrinks signal and adds fresh noise

Forward diffusion is a fixed Markov chain that progressively corrupts data with Gaussian noise.

$$x_k=\sqrt{1-\beta_k}\,x_{k-1}+\sqrt{\beta_k}\,z_k$$
$x_{k-1},x_k\in\mathbb R^d$
previous and next noisy vectors
$\beta_k\in(0,1)$
chosen variance of fresh transition noise
$\alpha_k=1-\beta_k$
one-step retention (MIT/DDPM convention)
$z_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)$
fresh noise, independent of previous states

DDPM §2, Eq.2 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Exercise

Forward diffusion

Check the conditional mean and covariance

Find the conditional mean and covariance of x_k.

$$x_k=\sqrt{1-\beta_k}\,x_{k-1}+\sqrt{\beta_k}\,z_k$$
$x_{k-1}∈R^d$
fixed previous state
$0<\beta_k<1$
fixed transition variance
$z_k\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)$
independent fresh noise

Check Mean $\sqrt{1-\beta_k}x_{k-1}$; covariance $\beta_k I$.

Solution 1 / 1

Conditioning fixes the input

$z_k$ has mean zero and covariance $I$.

  1. $\E[x_k\mid x_{k-1}]=\sqrt{1-\beta_k}\,x_{k-1}$.
  2. $x_k-\E[x_k\mid x_{k-1}]=\sqrt{\beta_k}z_k$.
  3. $\operatorname{Cov}(x_k\mid x_{k-1})=\beta_k I$.

DDPM Eq.2; DL §3.8 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Exercise

Forward diffusion

Transfer: variance is not the noise multiplier

Compute the realized x_k; show both coefficients.

$$\begin{aligned}x_k&=\sqrt{1-\beta_k}\,x_{k-1}+\sqrt{\beta_k}\,z_k\\ \beta_k&=0.36,\quad x_{k-1}=2,\quad z_k=-1\end{aligned}$$
$\beta_k$
variance
$x_{k-1},z_k$
given scalar values

Check $x_k=0.8(2)+0.6(-1)=1$.

Solution 1 / 1

Compute coefficients before the state

The fresh noise draw is $z_k=-1$.

  1. $\sqrt{1-\beta_k}=\sqrt{0.64}=0.8$, and $\sqrt{\beta_k}=0.6$.
  2. $x_k=0.8\times2+0.6\times(-1)=1.6-0.6=1$.
  3. Using 0.36 as the noise multiplier would give the wrong variance.

DDPM Eq.2; course exercise · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Derivation

Forward diffusion

Two steps expose the cumulative signal

$$x_2=\sqrt{\alpha_2\alpha_1}x_0+\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}z_1+\sqrt{\beta_2}z_2$$
$x_0,x_2$
clean and two-step noisy vectors
$\alpha_j=1-\beta_j$
one-step retention; beta is step noise variance
$z_1,z_2$
independent standard Gaussian noises

The first noise survives step two with coefficient $\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}$.

Derivation 1 / 1

Substitute the first transition into the second

$\alpha_j=1-\beta_j$. Independent $z_1,z_2$ are standard Gaussian vectors.

  1. $x_1=\sqrt{\alpha_1}x_0+\sqrt{\beta_1}z_1$.
  2. $x_2=\sqrt{\alpha_2}x_1+\sqrt{\beta_2}z_2$.
  3. $x_2=\sqrt{\alpha_2}(\sqrt{\alpha_1}x_0+\sqrt{\beta_1}z_1)+\sqrt{\beta_2}z_2$.
  4. $x_2=\sqrt{\alpha_2\alpha_1}x_0+\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}z_1+\sqrt{\beta_2}z_2$.

DDPM §2, Eq.4; course expansion · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Derivation

Forward diffusion

Independent Gaussian variances combine

$$\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2=(1-\beta_2)\beta_1+\beta_2=1-\alpha_1\alpha_2$$
$\alpha_j=1-\beta_j$
one-step retention; beta is step noise variance
$\bar\alpha_2=\alpha_1\alpha_2$
two-step cumulative retention
$z_1,z_2$
independent standard Gaussian noises

Independent noise variances add: $\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2=1-\bar\alpha_2$.

Derivation 1 / 1

Combine independent centered noise terms

The noise coefficients are $\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}$ and $\sqrt{\beta_2}$.

  1. $\operatorname{Cov}(\sqrt{\alpha_2\beta_1}z_1+\sqrt{\beta_2}z_2)=(\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2)I$.
  2. $\alpha_2\beta_1+\beta_2=(1-\beta_2)\beta_1+\beta_2=1-\alpha_1\alpha_2$.
  3. The sum is Gaussian. Replace it in distribution by a standard Gaussian scaled by the square root of one minus alpha bar at level two.

DDPM Eq.4; course derivation · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Result

Forward diffusion

Any noise level can be sampled directly

This is the conditional corruption law for one fixed clean vector.

$$x_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\epsilon,\quad\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$$
$\alpha_j=1-\beta_j$
one-step retention from step variance beta
$\bar\alpha_k=\prod_{j=1}^k\alpha_j$
cumulative retention, 0 < bar alpha <= 1
$\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k},\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$
signal and noise standard-deviation scales
$\epsilon$
fresh standard Gaussian, independent of x₀

DDPM Eq.4; after MIT 6.S978 Lecture 5 visual progression; course scalar diagram · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · MIT 6.S978, Lecture 5

Interpretation

Forward diffusion

A schedule controls signal-to-noise ratio

Signal-to-noise ratio compares signal variance with added noise variance.

$$\operatorname{SNR}_k=\frac{\bar\alpha_k}{1-\bar\alpha_k}$$
$\bar\alpha_k$
cumulative signal retention
$1-\bar\alpha_k$
added noise variance
$\operatorname{SNR}_k$
coefficient ratio for unit-variance clean signal

DDPM §4; Diffusion Policy §3.3 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Example

Forward diffusion

Worked example: one noisy training pair

Example

$$\begin{aligned}x_0&=2,\ \sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}=0.8,\ \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}=0.6,\ \epsilon=-0.5\\x_k&=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon=1.3\\\text{input}&=(1.3,k),\quad\text{target}=-0.5\end{aligned}$$
$x_0, x_k$
clean scalar; noisy scalar at level k
$\epsilon$
known sampled training noise
$\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k},\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$
signal amplitude; noise standard deviation

DDPM Algorithm 1; course example · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Exercise

Forward diffusion

Transfer: a two-component action

Compute the noisy vector $x_k$, then recover the sampled noise $\epsilon$.

$$x_0=\begin{bmatrix}2\\-1\end{bmatrix},\quad\epsilon=\begin{bmatrix}-0.5\\1\end{bmatrix},\quad\bar\alpha_k=0.64$$
$x_0,\epsilon\in\mathbb R^2$
clean and sampled-noise columns
$x_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$
noise scales are 0.8 and 0.6; k is diffusion level

Check $x_k=(1.3,-0.2)^T$ and the recovered sampled noise is $\epsilon=(x_k-0.8x_0)/0.6=(-0.5,1)^T$.

Solution 1 / 1

Apply the rule componentwise

$x,x_0,\epsilon$ are two-component columns; $[x]_i$ is component $i$, not diffusion level $i$.

  1. $[x]_1=0.8(2)+0.6(-0.5)=1.3$.
  2. $[x]_2=0.8(-1)+0.6(1)=-0.2$.
  3. $(x-0.8x_0)/0.6=(-0.5,1)^T=\epsilon$.

DDPM Eq.4; course exercise · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Exercise

Forward diffusion

The marginal covariance also contains data spread

Mean and covariance of X_k?

$$X_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}X_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon,\quad X_0\perp\epsilon$$
$X_0,X_k\in\mathbb R^d$
random clean/noisy vectors at level k
$\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k},\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$
fixed signal/noise scales
$\mu_0,\Sigma_0$
clean mean/covariance
$\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)$
independent of X₀

Check $\mu_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\mu_0$, $\Sigma_k=\bar\alpha_k\Sigma_0+(1-\bar\alpha_k)I$.

Solution 1 / 1

Average over examples and noise

$X_0$ is random; $\epsilon$ is independent and centered.

  1. $\E[X_k]=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\E[X_0]+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\E[\epsilon]=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}\mu_0$.
  2. $X_k-\mu_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}(X_0-\mu_0)+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$.
  3. $\operatorname{Cov}(X_k)=\bar\alpha_k\Sigma_0+(1-\bar\alpha_k)I$; cross terms vanish by independence.

DDPM Eq.4; DL §3.8 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Assumption

Forward diffusion

The terminal Gaussian is a schedule approximation

On the training-data scale, choose the final level so the residual clean contribution is negligible.

$$\begin{aligned}X_K&=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_K}X_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_K}\,\epsilon\\\sqrt{\bar\alpha_K}X_0&\approx0,\quad\bar\alpha_K\approx0\quad\Longrightarrow\quad X_K\approx\mathcal N(0,I)\end{aligned}$$
$K,\bar\alpha_K$
final diffusion level and its small cumulative retention
$X_0$
clean data; residual negligible on its typical scale
$\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$
independent standard Gaussian noise
$X_K$
terminal noisy vector; Gaussian claim is approximate

DDPM §4, terminal prior · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Exercise

Forward diffusion

Check the terminal prior

Standard normal?

$$\begin{aligned}\mathbb E[X_K]&=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_K}\,\mathbb E[X_0],\quad\operatorname{Var}(X_K)=\bar\alpha_K\operatorname{Var}(X_0)+1-\bar\alpha_K\\\bar\alpha_K&=0.64,\quad\mathbb E[X_0]=5,\quad\operatorname{Var}(X_0)=1\end{aligned}$$
$X_0,X_K$
random clean and noisy scalar data
$\bar\alpha_K=0.64$
signal scale 0.8; noise standard deviation 0.6
$\mathcal N(0,1)$
proposed generation prior

Check $\mathbb E[X_K]=4$ and $\operatorname{Var}(X_K)=1$: not standard normal (mean is not zero).

Solution 1 / 1

Use a necessary moment check

The added standard noise is independent of clean data.

  1. $\E[X_K]=0.8\times5=4$.
  2. $\operatorname{Var}(X_K)=0.8^2(1)+0.6^2=1$.
  3. A standard normal has mean zero. Matching its variance does not repair the mean mismatch.

DDPM §4; course exercise · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Definition

The score

A density supplies a local direction

The score is the gradient of log density with respect to the data vector.

$$s_k(x)=\nabla_x\log p_k(x)$$
$p_k(x)>0$
differentiable density at fixed noise level k
$s_k(x)\in\mathbb R^d$
input gradient; density parameters fixed

Hyvärinen (2005) §2, Eq.1; Vincent (2011) §3.1 · Vincent (2011) · Hyvärinen (2005)

Model

The score

Start with a Gaussian log density

$$\log p(x)=C-\frac{(x-\mu)^2}{2v}$$
$\mu\in\mathbb R,\ v>0$
fixed mean and variance
$C=-\tfrac12\log(2\pi v)$
constant with respect to x

DL §3.9.3; course derivation · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Derivation

The score

Differentiate the quadratic one step at a time

$$s(x)=-\frac{1}{2v}\,2(x-\mu)=-\frac{x-\mu}{v}$$
$\mu,v$
fixed mean and variance
$s(x)$
scalar score

For $v>0$, the scalar Gaussian score is $s(x)=-(x-\mu)/v$.

Derivation 1 / 1

Differentiate the scalar Gaussian log density

$\mu$ and variance $v>0$ are fixed; $C$ is constant in $x$.

  1. $\log p(x)=C-(x-\mu)^2/(2v)$.
  2. $\partial_x C=0$, and $\partial_x(x-\mu)^2=2(x-\mu)$.
  3. $s(x)=-[2(x-\mu)]/(2v)=-(x-\mu)/v$.

DL §3.9.3; course derivation · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Result

The score

Covariance shapes the vector direction

The precision matrix is the inverse covariance; it weights displacement in the Gaussian score.

$$s(x)=-\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$$
$x,\mu\in\mathbb R^d$
state and mean
$\Sigma\succ0$
fixed positive-definite covariance

For $\Sigma\succ0$, the vector Gaussian score is $s(x)=-\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$.

Derivation 1 / 1

Differentiate a symmetric quadratic form

$r=x-\mu$ is a column vector; positive-definite covariance $\Sigma$ is fixed.

  1. $\log p(x)=C-\tfrac12r^T\Sigma^{-1}r$.
  2. $d(r^T\Sigma^{-1}r)=dr^T\Sigma^{-1}r+r^T\Sigma^{-1}dr=2r^T\Sigma^{-1}dx$.
  3. $d\log p(x)=(-\Sigma^{-1}r)^Tdx$, so $s(x)=-\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$.

DL §3.9.3; Lecture 5 quadratic differential · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Exercise

The score

Compute an anisotropic score

Compute s(x). Is its direction parallel to −x?

$$\mu=\begin{bmatrix}0\\0\end{bmatrix},\ \Sigma=\begin{bmatrix}4&0\\0&1\end{bmatrix},\ x=\begin{bmatrix}2\\1\end{bmatrix}$$
$\Sigma$
covariance, not standard deviations
$s(x)=-\Sigma^{-1}(x-\mu)$
score to find

Check $s(2,1)=(-0.5,-1)^T$; this is not parallel to $-x=(-2,-1)^T$.

Solution 1 / 1

Apply the precision matrix

The inverse covariance is the precision matrix.

  1. $\Sigma^{-1}=\operatorname{diag}(1/4,1)$.
  2. $s(x)=-\operatorname{diag}(1/4,1)(2,1)^T=(-1/2,-1)^T$.
  3. The narrower second direction receives stronger correction per unit displacement.

DL §3.9.3; course exercise · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Derivation

The score

An unknown normalizing constant disappears

$$p(x)=\frac{e^{-E(x)}}{Z}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\nabla_x\log p(x)=-\nabla_x E(x)$$
$E(x)$
differentiable energy
$Z$
finite positive constant independent of x

Hyvärinen (2005) §2, Eq.1; course energy form · Hyvärinen (2005)

Derivation

The score

A mixture score combines component scores

A mixture averages densities. Responsibility is a component’s posterior weight at x.

$$s(x)=\sum_j r_j(x)s_j(x),\quad r_j(x)=\frac{w_jp_j(x)}{\sum_iw_ip_i(x)}$$
$w_j\ge0,\ \sum_jw_j=1$
fixed mixture weights
$p_j>0,\ s_j=\nabla_x\log p_j$
component density; score
$r_j(x)$
posterior component probability at x

At each $x$, $s(x)=\sum_j r_j(x)s_j(x)$ with $r_j(x)=w_jp_j(x)/p(x)$.

Derivation 1 / 1

Differentiate the sum before taking responsibilities

Fixed weights $w_j\ge0$ sum to one; component densities are differentiable.

  1. $p(x)=\sum_jw_jp_j(x)$, so $\nabla p(x)=\sum_jw_j\nabla p_j(x)$.
  2. $s(x)=\nabla p(x)/p(x)=\sum_j[w_jp_j(x)/p(x)]\,\nabla\log p_j(x)$.
  3. Set $r_j(x)=w_jp_j(x)/p(x)$ to obtain $s(x)=\sum_jr_j(x)s_j(x)$.

DL §3.9.6; course derivation · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Exercise

The score

What does a stationary point tell us?

Find s(0). Is x=0 a mode? Explain.

$$p(x)=\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;-2,1)+\tfrac12\mathcal N(x;2,1)$$
$x,\ \mu_1=-2,\ \mu_2=2$
scalar point and two component means
$s_j(x)=-(x-\mu_j)$
component score for variance one

Check $s(0)=0$, but $p^{\prime\prime}(0)>0$: $x=0$ is a local minimum, not a mode.

Solution 1 / 1

Opposing component directions cancel

At $x=0$, symmetry makes both responsibilities $1/2$.

  1. $s_1(0)=-(0+2)=-2$, $s_2(0)=-(0-2)=2$.
  2. $s(0)=\tfrac12(-2)+\tfrac12(2)=0$.
  3. Each Gaussian has $p_j^{\prime\prime}(0)=(2^2-1)p_j(0)$, so $p^{\prime\prime}(0)=3\mathcal N(0;2,1)>0$.

DL §3.9.6; course exercise · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Exercise

The score

Transfer: doubling standard deviation

Compare standard deviations 1 and 2. Compute both scores.

$$\mu=1,\quad x=3,\quad s(x)=-(x-\mu)/v$$
$x=3,\ \mu=1$
fixed point and Gaussian mean
$v,\ \sqrt v$
variance and standard deviation

Check Standard deviation $1\to2$ gives $s(3)=-2\to-0.5$.

Solution 1 / 1

Convert spread into variance

The displacement $x-\mu=2$ in both models.

  1. First: $v=1^2=1$, so $s(3)=-2$.
  2. Second: $v=2^2=4$, so $s(3)=-2/4=-0.5$.
  3. The wider log density changes less sharply at the same displacement.

DL §3.9.3; course exercise · Goodfellow et al. (2016)

Model

Learning to denoise

Known corruption gives a target for every example

Training constructs inputs from clean data and known noise; the sampled noise supplies the target.

$$(x_0,k,\epsilon)\longmapsto\big((x_k,k),\epsilon\big)$$
$x_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$
network input constructed from a clean example
$\epsilon$
known sampled noise used as the target
$k$
sampled diffusion level

DDPM §3; after MIT 6.S978 Lecture 5 training sequence; course diagram · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · MIT 6.S978, Lecture 5

Definition

Learning to denoise

The simple noise-prediction objective

Expected squared noise error.

$$L(\theta)=\E\|\epsilon_\theta(\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon,k)-\epsilon\|^2$$
$x_0,k,\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k},\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$
clean vector, level and fixed corruption coefficients
$\theta$
learned network parameters
$\epsilon_\theta,\epsilon\in\mathbb R^d$
predicted and sampled Gaussian noise
$\mathbb E$
average over data, uniform k and Gaussian noise

DDPM Eq.14; after MIT 6.S978 Lecture 5 training sequence; course diagram · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · MIT 6.S978, Lecture 5

Derivation

Learning to denoise

The optimal predictor is a conditional mean

$$\E[\|\epsilon-g\|^2\mid x_k,k]=\E[\|\epsilon-m\|^2\mid x_k,k]+\|g-m\|^2$$
$\epsilon,x_k,k$
sampled noise; fixed noisy input and level
$m=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_k,k]$
conditional mean-noise vector
$g\in\mathbb R^d$
chosen prediction

The noise-prediction MSE minimizer is $g^*=\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_k,k]$.

Derivation 1 / 2

Expand the vector squared distance

Fix $x_k,k$. Let $m=\E[\epsilon\mid x_k,k]$; assume a finite conditional second moment.

  1. $\epsilon-g=(\epsilon-m)+(m-g)$.
  2. $\|\epsilon-g\|^2=\|\epsilon-m\|^2+2(\epsilon-m)^T(m-g)+\|m-g\|^2$.

Derivation 2 / 2

Average and minimize

$m,g$ are fixed under this conditional expectation.

  1. $\E[(\epsilon-m)^T(m-g)\mid x_k,k]=0$.
  2. $\E[\|\epsilon-g\|^2\mid x_k,k]=\E[\|\epsilon-m\|^2\mid x_k,k]+\|g-m\|^2$.
  3. Only the last term depends on g, so $g^*=m$.

DDPM Eq.14; course least-squares derivation · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Derivation

Learning to denoise

One clean example has an accessible conditional score

For fixed x₀, qₖ is Gaussian with mean √ᾱₖ x₀ and covariance (1−ᾱₖ)I.

$$\nabla_{x_k}\log q_k(x_k\mid x_0)=-\frac{x_k-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0}{1-\bar\alpha_k}=-\frac{\epsilon}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}}$$
$x_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$
realized corruption
$x_0,k$
fixed; 0 < bar alpha < 1

Vincent (2011) §4.2, Eq.4.4; Gaussian score derivation · Vincent (2011)

Derivation

Learning to denoise

Average conditional scores to obtain the score

$$\nabla_x\log p_k(x)=\int p_k(x_0\mid x)\nabla_x\log q_k(x\mid x_0)\,dx_0$$
$q_k(x\mid x_0),p_k(x)>0$
corruption density; differentiable noisy marginal
$p_k(x_0\mid x)$
clean-data posterior at fixed k
$\mathrm{Assumption}$
differentiate under the integral

$s_k(x)=\mathbb E[\nabla_x\log q_k(x\mid X_0)\mid X_k=x]$.

Derivation 1 / 2

Differentiate the noisy marginal density

$q_k(x\mid x_0)$ is the Gaussian corruption density; $p_0$ is the clean density; fix $k$.

  1. $p_k(x)=\int p_0(x_0)q_k(x\mid x_0)\,dx_0$.
  2. $\nabla_xp_k(x)=\int p_0(x_0)\nabla_xq_k(x\mid x_0)\,dx_0$.
  3. The second equality assumes the derivative can pass under the integral.

Derivation 2 / 2

Divide by the marginal and apply Bayes rule

Assume $p_k(x)>0$. Bayes rule gives $p_k(x_0\mid x)=p_0(x_0)q_k(x\mid x_0)/p_k(x)$.

  1. $\nabla_x\log p_k(x)=\int \frac{p_0(x_0)q_k(x\mid x_0)}{p_k(x)}\frac{\nabla_xq_k(x\mid x_0)}{q_k(x\mid x_0)}\,dx_0$.
  2. $s_k(x)=\E[\nabla_x\log q_k(x\mid X_0)\mid X_k=x]$.
  3. For discrete clean support, replace the integrals by sums.

Vincent (2011) Appendix A, Eqs.A.1–A.2; course Bayes derivation · Vincent (2011)

Exercise

Learning to denoise

Noise prediction gives a score estimate

Explain the minus sign and the factor 1/√(1−ᾱₖ).

$$s_k(x)=-\frac{\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_k=x,k]}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}}\approx-\frac{\epsilon_\theta(x,k)}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}}$$
$s_k(x)$
true marginal noisy-data score
$\epsilon_\theta(x,k)$
learned conditional mean-noise prediction
$\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}>0$
fixed noise standard deviation at level k

Check $s_\theta=-\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$.

Solution 1 / 2

Join regression to the score identity

At fixed $k$, $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}>0$ is constant.

  1. $\nabla\log q_k=-\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$.
  2. $s_k=\E[\nabla\log q_k\mid x_k]= -\E[\epsilon\mid x_k]/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$.
  3. The MSE optimum is $\epsilon_\theta^*=\E[\epsilon\mid x_k]$.

Solution 2 / 2

Noise regression is a form of denoising score matching

Fix $k$; set $s_\theta=-\epsilon_\theta/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$, $c=\nabla_x\log q_k=-\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$.

  1. $\E\|\epsilon_\theta-\epsilon\|^2=(1-\bar\alpha_k)\E\|s_\theta-c\|^2$.
  2. $\E\|s_\theta-c\|^2=\E\|s_\theta-s_k\|^2+C_k$.
  3. $C_k=\mathbb E\|c-s_k(X_k)\|^2$ is the irreducible conditional target variance at fixed $k$, independent of $\theta$.

Vincent (2011) §4.2, Eqs.4.3–4.5; DDPM §3.2 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Vincent (2011)

Exercise

Learning to denoise

What can a zero noise prediction mean?

Find the noise for each clean hypothesis, then its mean.

$$X_0\in\{-1,1\},\quad\bar\alpha_k=1/2,\quad X_k=0$$
$X_0$
clean values −1,+1, each with probability 1/2
$X_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}X_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$
Gaussian epsilon independent of clean data; condition via density

Check The two possible sampled noises are $-1$ and $1$; their conditional mean is $0$.

Solution 1 / 1

Two explanations of one input

The symmetric likelihoods give equal posterior weights.

  1. If $X_0=1$, then $0=(1+\epsilon)/\sqrt2$, so $\epsilon=-1$.
  2. If $X_0=-1$, the required noise is $\epsilon=1$.
  3. $\E[\epsilon\mid X_k=0]=(-1+1)/2=0$.

DDPM Eq.14; course exercise · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Result

Learning to denoise

A denoising identity gives the posterior mean

Conditional clean mean from a noisy observation.

$$\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_k=x]=\frac{x+(1-\bar\alpha_k)s_k(x)}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}}$$
$X_0,X_k=x$
random clean data; observed noisy vector x
$0<\bar\alpha_k<1$
chosen cumulative retention
$s_k(x)$
true noisy-data score at x

$\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_k=x]=[x+(1-\bar\alpha_k)s_k(x)]/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.

Derivation 1 / 2

Invert the known corruption algebraically

$X_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}X_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$, with $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k},\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}>0$; condition on $X_k=x$.

  1. $X_0=(x-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.
  2. $\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_k=x]=(x-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid X_k=x])/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.
  3. The observed x is fixed inside this conditional expectation.

Derivation 2 / 2

Substitute the noise-score relation

The exact marginal score obeys $\E[\epsilon\mid X_k=x]=-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}s_k(x)$.

  1. $\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_k=x]=(x-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}[-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}s_k(x)])/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.
  2. $\mathbb E[X_0\mid X_k=x]=(x+(1-\bar\alpha_k)s_k(x))/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.
  3. This is a posterior mean, not a random sample or a guaranteed mode.

Efron (2011), Eq.1.4; scaled Tweedie identity · Efron (2011)

Exercise

Learning to denoise

How does predictor error reach the clean estimate?

Let Δx̂₀ = imperfect estimate − optimal estimate. Find it; compare signal scales √ᾱₖ = 0.8 and 0.1.

$$\hat x_0=\frac{x-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\,\hat\epsilon}{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}},\quad\hat\epsilon=\epsilon^*+\delta$$
$x=x_k\in\mathbb R^d$
fixed noisy input at diffusion level k
$\epsilon^*$
optimal conditional mean-noise prediction
$\delta\in\mathbb R^d$
prediction error at the same noisy input
$\bar\alpha_k>0$
cumulative retention; fixes signal/noise scales

Check $\Delta\hat x_0=-(\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k})\delta$.

Solution 1 / 1

Subtract the two estimates

Both estimates use the same $x$, $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$ and $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$.

  1. $\Delta\hat x_0=[x-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}(\epsilon^*+\delta)]/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}-[x-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon^*]/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.
  2. $\Delta\hat x_0=-(\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k})\delta$.
  3. Error magnitude is multiplied by $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$: $0.75$ at $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}=0.8$, and $\sqrt{0.99}/0.1\approx9.95$ at $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}=0.1$.

DDPM Eq.11; course exercise · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Exercise

Learning to denoise

Checkpoint: trace an input to a score

Data → known corruption → noise regression → score
Which quantity is sampled, observed, and learned?

Check Sample $x_0,k,\epsilon$; observe $(x_k,k)$; learn $\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_k,k]$ and infer its score.

Solution 1 / 1

Connect the four objects

At one training level, $\bar\alpha_k$ fixes both corruption scales.

  1. $x_0\sim p_0$, $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$; $x_k=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$.
  2. Input $(x,k)$; target $\epsilon$; population optimum $\E[\epsilon\mid x,k]$.
  3. $s_k(x)=-\mathbb E[\epsilon\mid x_k=x,k]/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}$.

DDPM Algorithm 1; Vincent (2011) §4.2, Eqs.4.3–4.5 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Vincent (2011)

Model

Reverse sampling

The reverse step needs a conditional distribution

The reverse conditional describes the previous state given the current noisy state. Here we also condition on the clean example to derive it.

$$q(x_{k-1}\mid x_k,x_0)\propto q(x_k\mid x_{k-1})q(x_{k-1}\mid x_0)$$
$x_0,x_k$
temporarily known endpoints
$x_{k-1}$
unknown intermediate state; k > 1

DDPM §2; CMU 10-423 Lecture 7 forward/reverse sequence; course diagram · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · CMU 10-423, Lecture 7

Derivation

Reverse sampling

The Gaussian product adds two quadratic penalties

$$-2\log q(y\mid x_k,x_0)=\frac{\|y-\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}x_0\|^2}{(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}+\frac{\|x_k-\sqrt{\alpha_k}y\|^2}{\beta_k}+C$$
$y=x_{k-1}$
unknown vector; k>1
$x_0,x_k$
fixed clean/noisy endpoints
$\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}},\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{k-1}}>0$
previous signal/noise scales
$0<\beta_k<1,\ \alpha_k=1-\beta_k,\ C$
step variance/retention; C fixed in y

DDPM Appendix A, posterior derivation · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Derivation

Reverse sampling

Complete the square

Complete the square in $y=x_{k-1}$; fix $x_0,x_k$, $k>1$.

$$\Lambda=\frac1{(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}+\frac{\alpha_k}{\beta_k},\quad h=\frac{\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}x_0}{(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_k}x_k}{\beta_k}$$
$\Lambda I$
posterior precision
$h$
coefficient vector
$\tilde\beta=1/\Lambda,\ \tilde\mu=h/\Lambda$
variance and mean

For $k>1$, $q(y\mid x_k,x_0)=\mathcal N(y;h/\Lambda,\Lambda^{-1}I)$.

Derivation 1 / 2

Expand and collect terms in the unknown state

$y=x_{k-1}$; $x_0,x_k$ are fixed and $(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})>0$.

  1. $\Lambda=1/(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})+\alpha_k/\beta_k$.
  2. $h=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}x_0/(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})+\sqrt{\alpha_k}x_k/\beta_k$.
  3. $-2\log q(y\mid x_k,x_0)=\Lambda\|y\|^2-2h^Ty+C$.

Derivation 2 / 2

Complete the square and read the Gaussian

$\Lambda>0$ is a scalar precision; $h$ is a column vector.

  1. $\Lambda\|y\|^2-2h^Ty+C=\Lambda\|y-h/\Lambda\|^2+C^\prime$.
  2. $\tilde\mu=h/\Lambda$, $\tilde\beta=1/\Lambda$.
  3. $q(y\mid x_k,x_0)=\mathcal N(y;\tilde\mu,\tilde\beta I)$.

DDPM Eqs.6–7; Appendix A · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Result

Reverse sampling

Simplify the posterior coefficients

$k>1$, $\bar\alpha_k=\alpha_k\bar\alpha_{k-1}$; $h=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}x_0/(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})+\sqrt{\alpha_k}x_k/\beta_k$.

$$\tilde\mu_k=c_0x_0+c_kx_k,\quad\tilde\beta_k=\frac{\beta_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_k}$$
$c_0=\beta_k\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}/(1-\bar\alpha_k)$
clean coefficient
$c_k=\sqrt{\alpha_k}(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})/(1-\bar\alpha_k)$
current noisy-state coefficient

$\tilde\beta_k=\beta_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})/(1-\bar\alpha_k)$ and $\tilde\mu_k=c_0x_0+c_kx_k$.

Derivation 1 / 1

Simplify the precision denominator

$\alpha_k=1-\beta_k$; $\bar\alpha_k=\alpha_k\bar\alpha_{k-1}$.

  1. $\Lambda=\frac{\beta_k+\alpha_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}{\beta_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}$.
  2. $\beta_k+\alpha_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})=1-\bar\alpha_k$.
  3. $\tilde\beta_k=1/\Lambda=\beta_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})/(1-\bar\alpha_k)$.
  4. $\tilde\mu_k=\tilde\beta_kh=c_0x_0+c_kx_k$.

DDPM Eq.7 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Derivation

Reverse sampling

Replace clean data by the learned noise estimate

$$\mu_\theta(x_k,k)=\frac1{\sqrt{\alpha_k}}\left(x_k-\frac{\beta_k}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}}\epsilon_\theta(x_k,k)\right)$$
$x_k,\hat\epsilon=\epsilon_\theta(x_k,k)$
current state; predicted noise
$\alpha_k=1-\beta_k$
one-step retention
$\bar\alpha_k=\prod_{j=1}^k\alpha_j$
cumulative retention
$\mu_\theta$
learned reverse Gaussian mean

$\mu_\theta(x_k,k)=[x_k-\beta_k\epsilon_\theta(x_k,k)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}]/\sqrt{\alpha_k}$.

Derivation 1 / 2

Insert the clean estimate into the known-clean mean

$\bar\alpha_k=\alpha_k\bar\alpha_{k-1}$ and $1-\bar\alpha_k$ is the cumulative noise variance.

  1. $\hat x_0=(x_k-\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\hat\epsilon)/\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}$.
  2. $\mu_\theta=\frac{\beta_k\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{k-1}}}{1-\bar\alpha_k}\hat x_0+\frac{\sqrt{\alpha_k}(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_k}x_k$.
  3. The noise coefficient becomes $-\beta_k/(\sqrt{\alpha_k}\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k})$.

Derivation 2 / 2

Simplify the remaining state coefficient

$\beta_k+\alpha_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})=(1-\bar\alpha_k)$.

  1. Coefficient on $x_k$: $[\beta_k+\alpha_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})]/(\sqrt{\alpha_k}(1-\bar\alpha_k))=1/\sqrt{\alpha_k}$.
  2. $\mu_\theta=(x_k-\beta_k\hat\epsilon/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k})/\sqrt{\alpha_k}$.
  3. With optimal mean-noise prediction this gives the reverse conditional mean; a fixed-variance Gaussian still approximates its full law.

DDPM §3.2, Eq.11 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

Reverse draw

Find draw and variance.

$$\tilde\beta_k=\frac{\beta_k(1-\bar\alpha_{k-1})}{1-\bar\alpha_k},\quad x_{k-1}=\mu_\theta+\sqrt{\tilde\beta_k}\,z$$
$\mu_\theta=1.025,\ z=-1$

Solution 1 / 1

Continue the same forward schedule

$\beta_k=.36$, $\alpha_k=.64$, $\bar\alpha_k=.36$; the cumulative noise standard deviation is $.8$.

  1. $\bar\alpha_{k-1}=.36/.64=.5625$.
  2. $\tilde\beta_k=.36(1-.5625)/.64=.24609375$.
  3. $\sqrt{\tilde\beta_k}\approx.4960784$; $x_{k-1}=1.025-.4960784=.5289216$.
  4. Across fresh draws, $\operatorname{Var}(x_{k-1}\mid x_k)=.24609375$ in this Gaussian model.

Algorithm

Reverse sampling

DDPM generation runs from noise to data

Draw $x_K\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$ at the noisiest level $K$. For $k=K,\ldots,1$, predict noise, compute $\mu_\theta$, and draw the next state. Network weights $\theta$ stay fixed; at $k=1$ return clean $x_0$ without fresh noise.

DDPM Algorithm 2; after CMU 11-785 Lecture 23 p66; course animation · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · CMU 11-785, Lecture 23

Exercise

Reverse sampling

Does a mean predictor force identical samples?

Same observation and trained weights.
Different initial Gaussian draws.
Must the final samples be identical?

Check Different initial draws can lead to different outputs; they need not be identical.

Solution 1 / 1

Follow the whole random process

The network is deterministic at a fixed input and level.

  1. $X_K$ is random, so $\mu_\theta(X_K,K)$ can vary.
  2. For stochastic reverse steps, fresh $z_k$ adds variation.
  3. A conditional mean at each state does not equal the unconditional mean of every final sample.

DDPM Algorithm 2; course exercise · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020)

$j<k,\ 0<\bar\alpha_k<\bar\alpha_j\le1$

Reverse sampling

A generalized step allocates fresh randomness

$$x_j=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_j}\hat x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_j-\rho_{k,j}^2}\,\hat\epsilon+\rho_{k,j}z$$
$j<k,\ \bar\alpha_j$
cleaner level and its cumulative retention
$z\sim\mathcal N(0,I)$
fresh standard Gaussian draw
$0\le\rho_{k,j}\le\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_j}$

Model

Reverse sampling

The eta parameter selects the stochasticity

Eta controls the amount of fresh noise added by a sampling step.

$$\rho_{k,j}=\eta\sqrt{\frac{1-\bar\alpha_j}{1-\bar\alpha_k}\left(1-\frac{\bar\alpha_k}{\bar\alpha_j}\right)}$$
$j<k,\ 0\le\eta\le1$

$\bar\alpha_j>\bar\alpha_k>0$
cumulative retentions at cleaner/noisier levels

Solution 1 / 1

Separate timing arithmetic from quality evidence

The hypothetical cost is 8 ms per sequential network evaluation.

Definition

Conditioning

The action distribution depends on observations

The conditional score is the input gradient of a log density with the observation held fixed.

$$s_k(x\mid o)=\nabla_x\log p_k(x\mid o)$$
$o$
fixed observation context
$x$
noisy action column vector
$k,\ p_k(x\mid o)>0$
fixed noise level; density differentiable in x

Diffusion Policy §2.3 · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Model

Conditioning

The denoiser has three inputs and one matching output

The denoiser maps noisy actions, a noise level and fixed observations to a same-shaped noise prediction.

$$\epsilon_\theta:\ (x_k,k,o)\longmapsto\hat\epsilon\in\mathbb R^d$$
$x_k\in\mathbb R^d$
noisy action sequence
$k,o$
noise level and encoded observations

Diffusion Policy §§2.3,3.1–3.2 · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Definition

Conditioning

Classifier-free guidance combines two predictions

Classifier-free guidance combines conditional and unconditional denoiser predictions to control the effect of a condition.

$$\hat\epsilon_g=\hat\epsilon_u+w(\hat\epsilon_c-\hat\epsilon_u)$$
$\hat\epsilon_c,\hat\epsilon_u$
conditional and null-context predictions
$w$
guidance scale; same x and k

Classifier-Free Guidance §3.2, Eq.6, Algorithms 1–2; w here = 1 + paper w · Ho & Salimans (2022)

Interpretation

Conditioning

Guidance changes the fixed-level density direction

At fixed k: this density interpretation assumes exact scores and a normalizable power product.

$$s_g=(1-w)s_u+ws_c=\nabla_x\log\!\left[p_k(x)^{1-w}p_k(x\mid o)^w\right]$$
$x\in\mathbb R^d$
noisy action vector at fixed diffusion level k
$o$
fixed observation context
$s_u,s_c$
unconditional and observation-conditioned scores
$p_k(x),p_k(x\mid o)$
unconditional and conditioned densities
$w$
guidance scale; the power product must be normalizable

At this fixed level, exact scores yield the field $s_g=\nabla_x\log[p_k(x)^{1-w}p_k(x\mid o)^w]$ when the product is normalizable.

Derivation 1 / 2

Convert the linear prediction rule into scores

Both predictions use the same noise scale $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}>0$.

  1. $\hat\epsilon_g=(1-w)\hat\epsilon_u+w\hat\epsilon_c$.
  2. $s_g=-\hat\epsilon_g/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}=(1-w)s_u+ws_c$.
  3. For exact scores, $s_g=\nabla_x[(1-w)\log p_k(x)+w\log p_k(x\mid o)]$.

Derivation 2 / 2

Combine logarithms with the necessary qualification

Assume the power product can be normalized.

  1. $s_g=\nabla_x\log[p_k(x)^{1-w}p_k(x\mid o)^w]$.
  2. This is a fixed-noise-level identity. It does not alone identify the final distribution of a finite guided sampler.
  3. The practical scale trades conditioning strength against diversity and artifacts.

Classifier-Free Guidance §3.2; convention bridge · Ho & Salimans (2022)

$\hat\epsilon_u=0.2,\ \hat\epsilon_c=-0.1$

$\bar\alpha_k=0.75$
noise standard deviation is 0.5
$w=0,1,2$
guidance scales to compare

Check For $w=0,1,2$: $(\hat\epsilon_g,s_g)=(0.2,-0.4),(-0.1,0.2),(-0.4,0.8)$.

Solution 1 / 1

Compute the difference and apply the scale

Conditional minus unconditional predicted noise is $-0.3$.

  1. $w=0$: $\hat\epsilon_g=0.2$, so $s_g=-0.4$.
  2. $w=1$: $\hat\epsilon_g=-0.1$, so $s_g=0.2$.
  3. $w=2$: $\hat\epsilon_g=-0.4$, so $s_g=0.8$; this extrapolates.

Classifier-Free Guidance §3.2; course exercise · Ho & Salimans (2022)

Model

Diffusion Policy

An action chunk is the vector being generated

The clean normalized chunk stacks dimensionless actions $u_r$; after denoising, convert them to physical commands $a_r$.

$$A_r^{(0)}=\begin{bmatrix}u_r^T\\\vdots\\u_{r+H_p-1}^T\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb R^{H_p\times d_a}$$
$r,\ u_r\in\mathbb R^{d_a}$
physical time and dimensionless normalized action column
$a_r$
physical action command after restoring units
$H_p,d_a$
prediction horizon and action dimension
$(0)$
clean diffusion level, not physical time

Read the original Diffusion Policy diagram

Exercise

Diffusion Policy

Three horizons serve different purposes

Count observations, predicted scalars, and executed steps.

$$H_o=2,\quad H_p=4,\quad H_a=2,\quad d_a=2$$
$H_o$
number of observations supplied
$H_p$
number of actions predicted
$H_a$
actions executed before replanning
$d_a=2$
scalar components per action

Check 2 observations; 8 predicted scalars; execute 2 steps.

Solution 1 / 1

Read each horizon in its own clock

Each of four predicted actions has two components.

  1. Observation input: two recent observations.
  2. Prediction: 4 × 2 = 8 scalar components.
  3. Execution: apply the first two actions, then obtain new observations and replan.

Diffusion Policy §2.3; course exercise · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Definition

Diffusion Policy

Train on demonstrated chunks

Squared Frobenius norm sums action errors; expectation averages data, levels and noise.

$$L(\theta)=\E\|\epsilon_\theta(A_r^{(k)},k,o_r)-\epsilon\|_F^2$$
$A_r^{(k)}=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_k}A_r^{(0)}+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_k}\epsilon$
noisy chunk; clean chunk is normalized
$o_r,\ r,\ k$
observation history at physical time r; k is diffusion level
$\epsilon,\epsilon_\theta\in\mathbb R^{H_p\times d_a}$
sampled noise and prediction
$\theta$
learned weights

Diffusion Policy §2.3, Eq.5; DDPM Eq.14 · Ho, Jain & Abbeel (2020) · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Exercise

Diffusion Policy

A receding horizon closes the feedback loop

Receding horizon: predict a chunk, execute its first H_a actions, then replan from fresh observations. What happens to the unused suffix?

Check Replan using fresh observations; do not blindly replay the old suffix.

Solution 1 / 1

Close the feedback loop

H_a is the number of actions executed before the next policy replan; learned weights stay fixed.

  1. Collect the current observation context, then denoise an initialized action chunk.
  2. Execute its first H_a actions using the robot controller.
  3. Refresh the context and generate a new chunk; the unexecuted suffix is not a commitment.

Diffusion Policy §2.3 · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Exercise

Diffusion Policy

Transfer: change execution without changing the sampler

Execution horizon H_a counts actions before replanning. Targets: 0.6 m, then 0.3 m. Compare H_a=1 and 2. An obstacle moves after the first action: which policy can refresh its second target?

Check Shorter execution horizon refreshes policy feedback sooner.

Solution 1 / 1

Separate generation from execution

The clean predicted chunk and sampler are unchanged.

  1. $H_a=1$: execute 0.6 m target, observe, then regenerate the next target.
  2. $H_a=2$: execute both planned targets before the policy replans.
  3. The first policy can incorporate the new observation earlier; neither horizon alone guarantees safety.

Diffusion Policy §2.3; course exercise · Chi et al. (2023/2024)

Exercise

Diffusion Policy

Training loss versus robot success

A diffusion model has low noise-prediction error on held-out Push-T demonstrations. The clip shows one rollout, but the policy fails in a new scene. Give one observation-side test and one execution-side test. What would each reveal?

Check Changed-view trials test observation shift; targets, units, timestamps and tracking test execution faults. Report success over repeated closed-loop trials.

Solution 1 / 1

Test the input and the physical loop

Held-out noise error measures prediction on demonstration chunks, not task success.

  1. Observation: compare camera views and object poses with the demonstrations, and test success in unseen scenes. A drop with changed views supports shift.
  2. Execution: log physical targets, timestamps and tracking. Wrong units or delays support an execution fault.
  3. Report success over repeated closed-loop trials; one clip is not a success rate.

Diffusion Policy project video; Diffusion Policy §§5,9; course exercise · Chi et al. (2023/2024)
